item.title: Why G7 agrees to release fuel reserves, how helpful will it be?
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
BRUSSELS, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Group of Seven (G7) leaders agreed Friday to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves in an action coordinated through the International Energy Agency (IEA), as surging fuel prices, disrupted refined-product supplies and threatened U.S. export restrictions added pressure on global energy markets. Under the agreement, the 100 million barrels will be released over four months, starting immediately, with a substantial amount of diesel to be frontloaded within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners. The G7 did not specify how much of the total would be diesel or crude oil, or how many individual countries would contribute. It said further diesel releases could be considered if necessary. IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said Friday that around 325 million barrels have so far been released under the collective action announced in March, representing more than 80 percent of the 400 million barrels originally pledged, the largest move of its kind in the agency's history. The group also agreed to coordinate refinery maintenance to avoid simultaneous shutdowns, temporarily raise refinery utilization where possible and encourage countries with significant refining capacity to increase production, particularly of diesel. Pressure has been acute in global fuel markets, particularly diesel, as two major sources of diesel and gasoil supply have been hit at the same time. Net diesel and gasoil exports from Gulf countries averaged just slightly more than a quarter of pre-U.S.-Iran war levels, as flows through the Strait of Hormuz remained severely constrained, according to the IEA. Birol also said that Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have added to the pressure on diesel supplies, pushing up prices. Europe has felt the strain acutely. The European Commission said Friday that diesel prices had doubled since the end of February when the U.S.-Iran war started, contributing to what it described as an "affordability crisis." EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen said Tuesday that the bloc had paid more than 100 billion euros (about 113.3 billion U.S. dollars) extra for fossil fuel imports since the start of the U.S.-Iran conflict, without receiving additional energy. The decision also followed mounting transatlantic friction over how to respond. The Trump administration had pressed European governments to draw down more emergency diesel stocks and warned that restrictions on U.S. diesel exports could follow if Europe did not act. The threat carried weight for Europe. The European Commission said last week that the United States accounted for around half of EU diesel imports in August, making the bloc highly exposed to any disruption in U.S. supplies. Hours before the G7 agreement, the Commission publicly rejected the prospect of a U.S. diesel export ban, saying such a move would benefit neither side and undermine trust in the United States as a reliable partner. The eventual G7 agreement combined coordinated reserve releases with a commitment to refrain from restricting energy exports among members, a move later welcomed by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Analysts say the release could provide meaningful short-term relief, particularly if large diesel volumes reach the market quickly. Alan Gelder, senior vice president for refining, chemicals and oil markets at Wood Mackenzie, estimated that a major diesel stock release could lower wholesale prices by 20 to 30 U.S. dollars per barrel. But the effect may prove temporary. Gelder said further stock releases essentially buy time while global diesel supply remains below demand and inventories continue to be drawn down, adding that the EU continues to be vulnerable to the export policies of others such as the United States. Ultimately, the longer-term stability of prices will depend on the restoration of refined-product flows from the Middle East. But with the U.S.-Iran conflict proving difficult to resolve, a swift return to more stable flows may remain out of reach. ■

item.title: Feature: "Auntie Basketball" brings Chinese culture to Utah high school
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-03
A member of "Auntie Basketball" talks with American students at Crimson Cliffs High School in Washington, Utah, the United States, Oct. 2, 2026.(Photo by Zeng Hui/Xinhua) by Xinhua Writer Gao Shan WASHINGTON, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Forget the traveling call, just run with the ball. Forget about winning or losing, just enjoy the game. Cheers, applause and laughter filled the gym at Crimson Cliffs High School in Washington, Utah, on Friday as a women's basketball team from Guizhou Province in southwestern China took on the school's team in a highly unusual game that brought together two groups of young people - and two cultures - on the same court. The visiting team, known as "Auntie Basketball," comes from a grassroots sporting tradition that originated in the Miao villages of Leishan County in southeastern Guizhou. In the Miao community, women who have married and returned to their hometowns are affectionately called "Gu Ma," or "aunties." What began as a recreational activity for women returning home has gradually grown into a showcase for Guizhou's ethnic culture and rural vitality. Unlike conventional basketball, Auntie Basketball has its own playful rules: Players can carry the ball and run with it rather than having to dribble. The result is less about the intensity of competition and more about fun, community and participation. Before the game, the gym came alive with songs from the Miao villages and energetic traditional dances. Dressed in colorful ethnic costumes, the visiting players performed for hundreds of students and teachers, drawing enthusiastic applause from the crowd. But the biggest excitement came when the players took the court. The aunties faced Crimson Cliffs' Mustangs, whose mascot is the mustang, in what quickly became a lighthearted cultural exchange through basketball. The American players initially struggled to adjust to the unusual rules, particularly the idea that they could run while carrying the ball instead of dribbling. But their solid fundamentals and teamwork soon kicked in. Fast-paced plays, quick passes and accurate shots kept the game lively, with the two teams trading baskets and giving the crowd plenty to cheer about. The chants from the stands grew louder: "Go, Gu Ma!" in Chinese and "Go, Mustangs!" in English. At one point, a tall Crimson Cliffs student dressed in a shirt and tie joined the aunties on the court. His exaggerated, "wild" and playful style of play sent the crowd into fits of laughter and pushed the atmosphere to another level. Reagan Haws, a Crimson Cliffs player, said that she found the game "really fun," especially because of the unusual rules. "It was just like a new experience. It was great to see the other cultures," she added. Crimson Cliffs Principal Kim Monkres welcomed the Chinese team to the school and said the visit provided an opportunity for cultural exchange between the two countries. "I'm just so thrilled that we have the opportunity to bring Chinese culture together with ours," she told Xinhua. "The dual language program in our school has been such a blessing. It's one of my favorite classes to sit in to. I have no idea what they're saying, but the kids do." Monkres said seeing how much the students have learned over the years and how fluent they have become in Chinese is "truly phenomenal." Monkres also expressed enthusiasm about China's plan to invite 100,000 young Americans to visit China for exchange and study programs over the next five years, saying she hopes Crimson Cliffs will have an opportunity to participate. Shen Xin, vice president of the Chinese People's Association for Friendship with Foreign Countries, who led the Auntie Basketball delegation to the United States, said the sport's grassroots and entertaining nature makes it an effective way to bring people from the two countries closer together. "It can help American people get a closer look at the everyday lives of ordinary people in China and learn more about the country's diverse ethnic cultures and traditions," Shen said, adding that he believes such people-to-people exchanges can help strengthen the foundation of China-U.S. relations. The Auntie Basketball team's U.S. tour, which began earlier this week, includes stops in California, Nevada, Utah and Washington state. ■ Members of "Auntie Basketball" pose for a group photo with an American student at Crimson Cliffs High School in Washington, Utah, the United States, Oct. 2, 2026.(Photo by Zeng Hui/Xinhua) Members of "Auntie Basketball" interact with American students at Crimson Cliffs High School in Washington, Utah, the United States, Oct. 2, 2026.(Photo by Zeng Hui/Xinhua)

item.title: Beyond mining tunnels: China's coal-rich province accelerates smarter, greener energy transition
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-03
TAIYUAN, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- From intelligent coal mines to digital power-grid management, north China's Shanxi Province is accelerating its energy transition and maintaining stable coal supplies. As one of China's major coal-producing provinces and a key national energy base, Shanxi is seeking to make its energy system smarter, more diversified and more efficient. The province is upgrading its traditional coal industry through smarter technologies and cleaner production, while expanding wind and solar power to diversify its energy mix. Backed by increasingly flexible power management, these efforts are reshaping how Shanxi produces, supplies and uses energy as China pursues greener development. AUTOMATED COAL MINING For 50-year-old Zhao Huacheng, deputy head of a fully mechanized mining team at Huayang New Material Technology Group Co., Ltd., a major coal mining enterprise in Shanxi, the transformation of coal mining is evident in his daily work. Zhao has worked in the industry for nearly 30 years, taking on almost every frontline role in his team, from coal miner and powered-support operator to safety officer. Huayang's No. 1 Mine, with an annual production capacity of 8.5 million tonnes, is among China's first batch of intelligent demonstration coal mines. Its intelligent mining faces use 5G technology and automated equipment to enable remote control and reduce the need for underground workers. The number of workers required underground for a shift at Zhao's team has already fallen from 24 to 16. Operating a coal-cutting machine was once one of the toughest jobs. Three operators had to work together, with one controlling the machine from a platform and the other two observing the terrain from the front and rear. When the machine started up, clouds of coal dust often made it nearly impossible to see, and flying chunks of coal posed a real risk of injury. Zhao still has a scar near his right eye as a reminder. "With advances in technology, the operator in the middle is no longer needed. The operators in front and behind can control the machine remotely from six meters away, reducing the risks," Zhao said. "We used to get bumped and bruised almost constantly. Now, such incidents are rare." Today, intelligent equipment has taken over most labor-intensive tasks. Clean mine tunnels, dust-suppression systems and enclosed control rooms have replaced the once dusty and hazardous working conditions. Productivity has also seen a sharp increase. A production shift that once yielded about 3,000 to 4,000 tonnes of coal can now produce 5,000 to 6,000 tonnes, according to Zhao. The transformation at Zhao's workplace is part of a broader push to make coal mining smarter and cleaner in Shanxi. By the end of November 2025, the province had built 369 intelligent coal mines, accounting for more than one-third of the national total, as well as 75 demonstration mines for green mining. On the national level, China aims to make virtually all types of coal mines intelligent by 2035 by leveraging advanced technologies, according to the National Development and Reform Commission. DIVERSIFIED ENERGY SUPPLY While making coal production smarter and cleaner, Shanxi is also reshaping its energy mix, with renewable energy becoming an increasingly important source of new capacity and power generation. At Shanxi Jinnan Steel Group Co., Ltd. in Quwo County, Linfen City, photovoltaic panels cover unused spaces ranging from rooftops and south-facing walls to hillside slopes and areas near an artificial lake. The company produces nearly 6 million tonnes of steel annually. Over the past five years, it has invested heavily in clean energy projects to reduce the carbon intensity of its energy consumption. Three months ago, the company partnered with PowerChina New Energy Group Co., Ltd. to develop green electricity by tapping the region's mountainous and valley resources. The two sides plan to use a "green electricity direct supply" model to better match the company's energy needs. "We have developed photovoltaic projects with a combined capacity of 550 megawatts, generating more than 1 billion kWh of electricity annually," said Zhang Tianfu, president of Shanxi Jinnan Steel Group Co., Ltd. Green electricity currently accounts for 15 percent of the company's power consumption. Zhang said the company will continue expanding its renewable energy portfolio and plans to raise the share to 50 percent by 2029. The company's growing investment in green electricity comes as renewable energy has become the main source of newly added power generation capacity and electricity generation in Shanxi. By the end of June this year, the province's installed capacity of wind and solar power had exceeded 80 million kW. In 2020, roughly one in every seven kWh generated in Shanxi came from renewable sources. Today, despite a substantial increase in total power generation, the share has risen to one in every four kWh. A historic shift has taken place in Shanxi's energy mix. By the end of September last year, installed capacity of new and clean energy sources accounted for 54.55 percent of the province's total, marking a historic shift from a fossil-fuel-dominated energy mix toward one led by clean energy. SMARTER POWER MANAGEMENT As wind and solar power generation expands, Shanxi faces a new challenge: how to accommodate increasingly variable renewable generation while keeping the power grid stable. Virtual power plants are emerging as one solution. Shanxi Fengxingcekong Co., Ltd. operates China's first virtual power plant participating in the electricity spot market. Nan Dou, deputy general manager of the company, said the spot market generates a new electricity price every five minutes. The virtual power plant aggregates scattered electricity-consuming resources and dispatches them through a digital platform, using algorithms to adjust the power loads of participating enterprises in response to changes in electricity prices and grid demand. "When electricity prices are low and renewable power generation is high, we encourage enterprises to consume more electricity, maximizing the use of renewable power. When prices are high and the grid is under pressure, we organize enterprises to reduce their loads during peak periods, helping ensure safe and stable grid operation," Nan said. "This benefits all three sides by ensuring power supplies, facilitating renewable power consumption and reducing energy costs for enterprises," he added. From August 2023 to June 2026, the virtual power plant helped facilitate the consumption of 350 million kWh of renewable electricity, equivalent to reducing carbon dioxide emissions by about 350,000 tonnes, the operators said. It also saved about 210 million kWh of electricity. Over the three years since entering the electricity market, the company's ability to aggregate and dispatch resources has continued to improve. The number of users on its platform has risen from five to more than 60, while its aggregated capacity has jumped from 80,000 kW to 2.282 million kW. "The most important improvement is that our control success rate has risen from 33 percent to 80 percent. Only by improving the quality of regulation can we achieve the desired results," Nan said. As of September 2026, 14 virtual power plants in Shanxi had participated in market trading, aggregating 1,459 users. Their combined capacity in the Shanxi electricity market had reached 6.4548 million kW, with a maximum adjustable load of 1.545 million kW. Traditional coal-fired power plants are also undergoing flexibility upgrades in response to market signals. The upgrades allow them to reduce output when wind and solar generation is abundant, creating more room for renewable power, and quickly ramp up output when renewable generation falls short, helping ensure electricity supplies. More than half of Shanxi's coal-fired power generating units have completed such flexibility upgrades. "Guided by market needs, Shanxi's renewable electricity utilization rate has remained above 90 percent," said Zhang Chao, an official in charge of the spot market at the Dispatching and Control Center of State Grid Shanxi Electric Power Co., Ltd. ■

item.title: A taste of home in orbit: How China keeps its astronauts well-fed
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-03
by Xinhua writer Yuan Quan BEIJING, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Although called Tiangong, or "Heavenly Palace," China's space station is becoming less distant and more like home, as astronauts bring the comforting tastes into orbit. The Chinese space kitchen now serves nearly 200 food items. Alongside dumplings and mooncakes, home-style dishes such as Kung Pao chicken, mapo tofu and fried rice have made it onto the station's menu. Videos showing astronauts savoring freshly cooked meat and cakes in orbit have gone viral. Their smiling faces and bright eyes make the aroma almost leap off the screen. Yang Liwei, the country's first astronaut, joked at a recent press conference that he was envious. He said astronauts can now use air-frying equipment in space and enjoy baked chicken wings in orbit. During his Shenzhou-5 mission in 2003, which lasted less than one day, his diet was limited to packaged instant food that could not be heated. Microgravity, cosmic radiation and the enclosed cabin environment impose strict requirements on space diets. Floating particles and droplets may drift into instruments and trigger malfunctions. Since Yuri Gagarin, the first human to travel into space, paste-like food and compressed energy bars had long served as the standard meals for astronauts. In June 2013, Wang Yaping, together with two fellow male crewmates, carried out the 15-day Shenzhou-10 space mission. People remembered this female astronaut with a ponytail for her space lecture. At the same time, the image of her floating a "zongzi," a leaf-wrapped rice dumpling, by hand also left a deep impression on the public. Zongzi is traditionally enjoyed during the Dragon Boat Festival, which happened to coincide with the Shenzhou-10 mission that year. To help the astronauts celebrate, this special snack was added to the spaceship pantry. Eight years later, Wang spent Spring Festival aboard the Tiangong space station during the Shenzhou-13 mission. It is also China's first six-month-long space stay. Scientists customized the cuisine: for instance, they prepared dumplings with seafood fillings because Wang grew up by the sea, and plenty of spicy food for crew member Ye Guangfu, who was born in chili-obsessed Sichuan Province. At that time, the core module Tianhe had several sections, including those for working, sleeping, dining and exercising. The videos of Shenzhou-13 crew practicing calligraphy and playing Taichi became social media hits. China completed the construction of its space station in 2022, with one core module and two lab modules forming a 110-square-meter orbital structure. Oxygen can be fully regenerated, and water recovery exceeds 95 percent. Since then, long-duration spaceflights have become routine, and the Chinese "space home" can host up to six astronauts in orbit at a time. Space residency is also set to last even longer. One member of the Shenzhou-23 crew, currently aboard the Tiangong, will conduct a one-year in-orbit stay. Moreover, as China pushes further into deep-space exploration, these extended stays will become the norm, which means astronauts' diets will be more important than ever. Because weightlessness causes bone calcium loss and muscle atrophy, space food must be high in calcium and protein, low in sodium and balanced in dietary fiber. According to the Astronaut Center of China, researchers have developed space food that counteracts oxidative damage, supports immunity, reduces fatigue and regulates the gut microbiome. But taste is another problem. In microgravity, blood shifts upward, causing nasal congestion and cutting smell sensitivity by at least 30 percent. Since taste is closely tied to smell, astronauts often find food bland. The center's researchers have responded with adding more strong-flavored dishes, with liquid soy sauce and concentrated chili sauce. New technology has also played a big role in keeping astronauts well-fed. The astronaut center, in collaboration with private companies, has upgraded the "space kitchen" with a suite of intelligent appliances for drinking water, food reheating and baking. This allows astronauts in orbit to enjoy hot meals within 20 minutes, rather than waiting longer or eating cold food. Liu Weibo, an expert with the center, gave an example of the hot-air baking oven, which is a pioneering Chinese design for space use that can efficiently remove cooking fumes and allow astronauts to enjoy barbecue in orbit. During a space lecture for Hong Kong and Macao students last month, Shenzhou-23 crew member Li Jiaying, or Lai Ka-ying in Cantonese, showed freshly baked cakes and said they reminded her of egg waffles, a popular snack from her hometown. She is a Hong Kong local. Space food supplies have also become more diverse and nutritious, including more fruits and vegetables, as well as frozen steak and chicken wings. The next-generation cargo craft Qingzhou, designed for future in-orbit supply delivery, will have greater cold-chain transport capacity. However, long-term space residency requires reducing dependence on Earth's supplies, said center expert Bian Qiang. "The controlled ecological life-support tests we are conducting are intended to build an ecosystem in space that regenerates water, air and food on site, to reduce extraterrestrial survival's dependence on Earth resupply and ultimately achieve self-sufficiency." Since the Shenzhou-16 mission in 2023, China has been growing plants in orbit. It has tested more than 20 varieties from 14 plant species, including lettuce, carrots, potatoes and wheat. The Shenzhou-18 crew in 2024 was tasked with raising fish in an "aquarium" to study how space affects their growth. Scientists said the work may one day allow astronauts to enjoy fish from their own in-orbit harvests. China is targeting a crewed lunar landing by 2030. Living on the moon will make resupply much more challenging because of the increased distance from Earth. "We plan to build a Chinese 'lunar vegetable garden' on the moon," Bian said. From heating, baking to farming, feeding astronauts well in space is not a luxury. It is part of the mission, bringing a taste of home to the universe. ■

item.title: Once upon a time in Iraq: Food, war, and the pursuit of peace
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-03
by Xinhua writers Wang Meiqi, Wang Xiaopeng and Yang Yuanyuan BEIJING, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- In the closing scene of the hit Chinese film "Once Upon a Time in the Middle East," sunlight fills a post-war restaurant as a waiter introduces the house specialty, namely "Xu Fu Rice Stew," a humble dish born out of wartime hardship. It begins as a simple pot of braised rice, made by a Chinese cook named Xu Fu for hungry children fleeing a regional fight. Yet the dish holds something deeper -- a shared hope for peace. The waiter is played by Ameen Muneer Mohammed Al-Obaidi, an Iraqi who goes by the Chinese name Fang Haoming. He is a young reporter and a survivor of the Iraq War launched by the United States. In 2003, when American missiles lit up the night sky over his hometown Baghdad, Al-Obaidi was barely three years old. "The only food we had then was raw potatoes and rock-hard flatbread. Even that wasn't guaranteed," he recalled. "My father would queue for hours to get two or three potatoes for the family." "When I saw the rubble and graffiti on set, it brought everything back," said Al-Obaidi. He moved to Yinchuan, the capital city of northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, in 2011 to reunite with his elder sister. She had married a Chinese man she met in the Middle East and later settled down in Yinchuan. "Before I came to China, I didn't know what peace was," he said. A few days after Al-Obaidi settled in the Chinese city, he encountered the Spring Festival, which is China's most important traditional festival, when families gather for reunion and celebration. At night, the sound of firecrackers and fireworks startled the Iraqi family. "Where I come from, when you hear that sound, everyone tenses up and wants to get into a bomb shelter," Al-Obaidi noted. But what he saw outside was very different: children laughing and cheering, families holding each other as colorful fireworks lit up the sky. "That was the first time I realized such sounds can bring happiness, not necessarily fear," he added. Ever since, the Spring Festival has been Al-Obaidi's favorite holiday, and he makes sure to have Chinese New Year's Eve dinner with family and friends every year. "Being able to sit down to a peaceful meal is the greatest joy for us," the young man said. This idea lies at the heart of the film. According to Wen Muye, the film's director, the decision to tell a war story through a restaurant came from a simple contrast: war brings destruction, while food is closely associated with warmth, reunion and everyday happiness. The film follows Xu's journey to the Middle East to work in a Chinese restaurant after falling into debt at home. Alongside restaurant manager Ma Junsheng, he helps build a popular eatery that becomes a gathering place for people from diverse backgrounds. Then war breaks out, and the restaurant, once a place of ordinary life, gets caught up in the violence. The film frequently returns to the theme of cooking, from dumplings made before Xu leaves home to a wedding banquet where Chinese and Arab food traditions come together. Later, as Xu flees the fighting with a group of orphaned children, he prepares a simple pot of rice. The meal is modest, Wen said, but for the frightened children, it offers something more important, providing a moment of security and a taste of normal life. The dish eventually becomes known as Xu Fu's braised rice at the restaurant. Since its release in August, the film has generated strong box-office numbers and positive reviews, grossing over 2.3 billion yuan (about 343 million U.S. dollars). Though set in the Middle East, the war drama's emotional center lies elsewhere. It can be found in the universal desire for an ordinary life, where a person can eat, work and sit together with family without fear. "Don't forget to eat properly" is an everyday Chinese expression of care. In the film, it becomes something much larger, a reminder of the normal life war threatens to take away. Though Al-Obaidi had never acted before this film, Wen was determined to cast the young Iraqi who had lived through war and embraced peace. Explaining his rationale, Wen said, "Just him standing there is the best performance." CHINESE RESTAURANT IN WARTIME BAGHDAD The Loong Restaurant, where Xu works as a chef in the hit film, also draws on real-life stories. For decades, running restaurants has been one of the most common ways Chinese people make a living overseas, and some Chinese restaurants have become unexpected meeting places between cultures. Chen Xianzhong, an Arabic-language graduate who first visited Iraq in 1984, left his stable job in a Chinese state-owned company years later and opened a Chinese restaurant named Yan Loong Wan in downtown Baghdad in 2003. At the time, it was one of just a few Chinese restaurants in the city. As Iraq is a Muslim-majority country, Chen said, he made sure that all the ingredients used in the restaurant were in line with local customs and acceptable to Muslim diners. Then the Iraq War broke out, and Chen nonetheless refused to give up his business. In a city where explosions shattered windows and fear emptied the streets, the restaurant became something rare: a taste of normal life. Diners could find authentic Chinese dishes, including dumplings, alongside local specialties such as samoon, a type of bread common in Iraq. Local Iraqi families, international journalists and diplomats, and even American soldiers arriving in armored vehicles, all came to eat, Chen said, adding that the restaurant put him in touch with many walks of life. When car bombs eventually made the city too dangerous to live in, Chen closed the restaurant in 2005 and sent his Chinese staff home. But he chose to stay, continuing to run a hotel and a shopping mall. "I had already got to know the country, and I could use the language I learned every day," he told Xinhua when explaining his decision to stay in Iraq despite the conflict. For Chen, opportunity and risk went hand in hand, and he was prepared to take that risk. "Almost every penny I earned came from Iraq," the 72-year-old said. "Now I just want to give something back -- to the Iraqi people and to my fellow Chinese." Hospitality, Chen recalled, is woven into the fabric of Iraqi life. His neighbors, some of them farmers with orchards, would drop by with fresh dates and sometimes even an entire grilled fish. "I've been to many places in the Middle East, and Iraq is my favorite. People there are very friendly to the Chinese," he said, adding that he often gives his neighbors Chinese porcelain products as tokens of appreciation for their kindness. Chen's real-life story echoes one of the film's central ideas: even in times of conflict, ordinary people keep looking for places to eat, talk and connect. LONGSTANDING TIES China and Arab countries boast a long history of friendly exchanges. For centuries, Chinese and Arab civilizations have traveled along the land and maritime Silk Roads, exchanging goods, knowledge and ideas across vast distances. For Al-Obaidi, the young Iraqi who grew up in China, the warmth he has experienced across cultures is part of this longer history. China and the Arab world may lie far apart on the map, he said, but they share the same reverence for peace and yearning for a better life, cherishing family and hospitality alike. When Al-Obaidi finally returned to Baghdad in 2024, he found construction cranes rising where shells once fell. Chinese companies are among those contributing to the rebuilding of his homeland, including by building schools. "Looking at those children's smiling faces, I recalled my childhood, and at that moment, I was convinced that the future of Iraq would be different," he said. On his third visit to China this June, former Iraqi President Abdul Latif Rashid spoke highly of China's constructive role in Iraq's post-war reconstruction and expressed gratitude for China's valuable support in energy, infrastructure and other areas. Speaking to Xinhua on the sidelines of the 2026 Forum on Global Human Rights Governance in Beijing in June, Rashid commended China's efforts to improve international relations and advance human rights. Drawing on Iraq's own experience, he observed that his country has endured decades of war, sanctions and terrorism, which has convinced him that peace and stability are the prerequisites for development, and development in turn is the bedrock of human rights. Today, around 10 Chinese restaurants operate in Baghdad, said Chen, who recently returned to Beijing. He noted that restaurants serving Middle Eastern cuisines can now be found in Beijing while Iraqi dates are available in China through online shops. According to him, Chinese household goods have also found a growing market in Iraq, with tableware and everyday porcelain products particularly popular. Such exchanges, he noted, go well beyond food. New-energy vehicles are also beginning to appear on Iraqi roads, with cars from Chinese brands becoming increasingly visible, he said. For Al-Obaidi, who speaks fluent Chinese, China is the place where he was reborn. He now works for an Arabic-language satellite broadcaster, covering China-Arab relations. "China has always worked to bring peace to the world. That is not empty diplomatic language. It is a fact I have felt with my own life," he said. Perhaps that is why a simple line in the film carries such weight. When Xu Fu tells the children to "eat properly," it is more than a reminder to finish a meal. It is a wish for something most people take for granted: a warm meal at the end of the day, a family gathered around the table, and children growing up without learning to fear the sound of explosions. Eat well. Live in peace. ■

item.title: Day 14 roundup: China achieves best result at overseas Asiad, Wong wins historic tennis gold
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-03
by sportswriter Li Jia NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- China reached 169 gold medals at the 2026 Asian Games after Saturday's penultimate day of competition, surpassing its previous record for the most golds won at an overseas edition of the Games. China won both the men's and women's golf team titles, with the men's victory delivering the delegation's 166th gold and breaking the previous overseas record of 165 set at the 2006 Games in Doha. Li Wenqi added another gold in women's windsurfing, while Guo Pu won the B-Girls breaking title. Defending champion Liu Qingyi took bronze. China also won the group all-around title as rhythmic gymnastics made its Asian Games debut, finishing ahead of host Japan and bronze medalist Kazakhstan. Uzbekistan's Takhmina Ikromova successfully defended her individual all-around title, with China's Wang Qi and Wang Zilu taking silver and bronze, respectively. "I'm happy that I was able to perform all four of my routines well today. I still had some small mistakes, but I'm happy I made it to the end and that it was enough for my second Asian Games gold," Ikromova said. In tennis, Coleman Wong became the first player from Hong Kong, China to win an Asian Games gold medal in the sport, beating China's Wu Yibing 6-2, 6-4 in the men's singles final. The victory also secured Wong a place at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. Wong broke Wu twice to take control of the opening set. The second remained level at 4-4 before Wong broke serve in the ninth game and served out the match. "Before the Games started, I was just hoping to win a medal, regardless of the color. But honestly, now reaching this point, winning this medal, you can call it unlocking an achievement," said Wong, 22. Wu took his second Asian Games silver medal, having also finished runner-up at Jakarta in 2018. On the football pitch, South Korea edged Japan 1-0 in the men's final, while China ended a 28-year wait for an Asian Games men's football medal by beating Uzbekistan 4-3 on penalties in the bronze-medal match after a 2-2 draw. It was also China's first medal in the event since the Asian Games men's football tournament adopted an under-23 format in 2002. China goalkeeper Li Hao saved two penalties in the shootout before Peng Xiao converted the decisive spot kick. China took silver in both rugby sevens events. The men's team achieved its best Asian Games finish despite losing 26-0 to Hong Kong, China in the final, while the women's team fell to Japan. Japan continued its dominance of women's softball with a 7-0 victory over China to claim its seventh consecutive Asian Games title. In beach volleyball, Qatar's Cherif Samba and Ahmed Janko came from behind to beat their Indonesian opponents 2-1 and secure a third successive Asian Games men's title. China took silver in the women's 57kg and over-67kg taekwondo events, finishing its campaign in the sport with one gold and two silvers. China missed out on a medal in men's volleyball after losing 3-0 to Pakistan in the bronze-medal match. Pakistan claimed its first Asian Games medal in the event in 64 years, while Iran beat Japan 3-1 in the final to secure a fourth consecutive title. The International Testing Agency also reported two more doping cases Saturday. India's kurash athlete Yash Kumar Chauhan and Uzbekistan rugby player Umar Usmonov have been provisionally suspended after testing positive for banned substances. The final two equestrian gold medals will be decided Sunday. China leads the medal table with 169 golds, 89 silvers and 83 bronzes. Japan is second with 83 golds, 95 silvers and 91 bronzes, followed by South Korea with 39 golds, 43 silvers and 68 bronzes. ■

item.title: China launches anti-dumping probe into EU p-Nitrotoluene imports
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-03
BEIJING, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- China has launched an anti-dumping investigation into imports of p-Nitrotoluene from the European Union (EU), the Ministry of Commerce said Saturday. According to the ministry's statement, it received a formal application on Sept. 14, 2026, from two domestic producers representing China's p-Nitrotoluene industry, requesting an anti-dumping investigation into imports from the EU. In response to a media query, a ministry spokesperson said preliminary evidence submitted by the applicants showed that the volume of p-Nitrotoluene imports from the EU remained at a high level from 2022 to 2025, with prices falling by nearly 60 percent cumulatively over the period. The dumped imports from the EU caused damage to the production and operations of China's domestic industry, the spokesperson said. The spokesperson pointed out that the application met the requirements for initiating an anti-dumping investigation under Chinese law and World Trade Organization rules, adding that China will conduct the investigation in accordance with relevant laws and regulations, fully protect the rights of all interested parties, and render an objective and impartial ruling. Noting that China has consistently taken a prudent and restrained approach to trade remedy measures, the spokesperson said the EU has launched 28 trade remedy investigations against China since 2025, about half of them involving chemical products, including three recent consecutive investigations into Chinese chemical products such as polyvinyl chloride. China has repeatedly called on the EU to face up to its own economic and trade issues and address each other's concerns through dialogue and consultation, the spokesperson said. According to the statement, the investigation began on Saturday and is expected to conclude before Oct. 3, 2027. It may be extended by six months under special circumstances. P-Nitrotoluene, also known as 4-Nitrotoluene, is mainly used to produce chemicals that are widely applied in dyes, pigments, pesticides, and pharmaceuticals, according to the ministry. ■

item.title: Extended breaks, richer experiences add momentum to China's holiday travel boom
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-03
BEIJING, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- China's National Day travel market kicked off on a strong note, as many travelers linked the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day breaks with their annual leave. This trend has led to longer trips and a surge in bookings for long-haul journeys, multi-city itineraries and experience-based travel products. LONGER BREAKS, FARTHER JOURNEYS With the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day separated by only three working days this year, some travelers used three days of leave to link the two breaks into a 13-day holiday. Trip.com Group data showed that one in every 10 travelers combined the two holidays into an extended break. Cao Shuai, CEO of Tongcheng Travel's destination business division, said strong demand for the 13-day break has lengthened the overall consumption cycle and helped release demand for long-haul and in-depth travel. Data from online travel platform Qunar showed that by Oct. 1, the first day of the National Day holiday, 20 percent of travelers had already reached the second city on their itineraries. Nearly 30 percent had booked hotels in at least two cities, while bookings involving stays in four or more cities surged 53 percent year on year. For Yuan You, who works for an internet company, the 13-day break made it possible to split one holiday into two distinct stages. She planned to first spend three days in Jiuzhaigou, a UNESCO-listed scenic area in southwest China's Sichuan Province known for its turquoise lakes and waterfalls, before continuing to Chengdu for the remainder of the break. "With such a long break, spending the whole time either resting or sightseeing can become monotonous, so I opted for a mix of both," Yuan said. In Chengdu, she chose to spend part of that extra time learning woodworking. Longer breaks are encouraging people to travel farther. Flight bookings for journeys of more than 2,000 km rose 76 percent year on year during the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day period, accounting for more than a quarter of all flight bookings, according to Meituan. Wang Peng, an associate researcher at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, said the extended break has encouraged more people to start traveling earlier, spreading trips over a longer period rather than concentrating them within a few peak days. That, Wang said, could help sustain demand across tourism, accommodation and catering services for longer periods of time. China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway) said that China's railway network handled 25.204 million passenger trips on Oct. 1, setting a new single-day record. RICHER EXPERIENCES, MORE TO EXPLORE The surge in mobility has translated into demand for richer experiences at destinations. At the National Maritime Museum of China in north China's Tianjin Municipality, 19,000 visitors streamed through the doors on the opening day of the National Day break. Among the new draws is "Echoes of the Whale Song," the museum's first customized full-sensory virtual reality experience. Unlike conventional walk-through VR attractions, visitors remain seated as the experience unfolds around them, allowing for a more immersive encounter. Under blue lights, visitors see a giant whale entangled in discarded fishing nets and take part in a virtual rescue, learning along the way about the impact of marine debris on ocean life. Such experience-oriented products are gaining traction well beyond one museum. On Fliggy, Alibaba Group's online travel platform, domestic attraction ticket bookings on Oct. 1 rose nearly 30 percent year on year, while the number of users purchasing products for natural scenic areas and villages increased by nearly 50 percent. Searches on Qunar for "immersive performances," "fireworks shows" and "night tours" also climbed more than 50 percent year on year. The growing demand for interactive travel experiences can be seen at Changchun Zoological and Botanical Park in northeast China's Jilin Province. There, a nighttime immersive show inspired by the Chinese classic "Journey to the West" has drawn large crowds into a vibrant fantasy world, with costumed performers mingling with visitors and transforming the park into a stage after dark. Yang Han, a researcher with Qunar's big data research institute, said travelers are increasingly setting out to "enter a story" rather than simply view static scenery, with content-driven experiences gaining popularity and bringing new opportunities to less traditional tourism destinations. Bu Xiting, an associate researcher in the School of Cultural Industries Management at Communication University of China, contrasted the current trend with the previously popular "special forces-style tourism," a fast-paced form of travel in which people try to pack as many sights as possible into a short period, and city walks, which offer smaller-scale urban experiences during pockets of free time. By linking public holidays with annual leave, travelers now have more time to shape their trips around what they want to experience, Bu said. Tourism consumption, Bu noted, is shifting from a focus on "time efficiency" toward greater "experience density."■
